prompt: What does the course text call the entire process of building, deploying, using and updating an information system?
explanation: Building, deploying, using and updating, the whole life of the system, is the SDLC.

why.a: Correct. That is the text's definition of the SDLC.
why.b: Wrong. Functional decomposition is dividing a system into subsystems.
why.c: Wrong. Requirements discovery is identifying problems and requirements with users, one part of analysis.
why.d: Wrong. Process modelling documents a system's processes, mainly with DFDs.

prompt: Which two of these are among the NINE principles of successful systems development in the course text?

options.text: Never cancel a project once it has started
Design systems for growth and change
Finish all documentation before speaking to users

explanation: The nine: get the user involved; use a problem-solving approach; establish phases and activities; establish standards; justify systems as capital investments; do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope; divide and conquer; design for growth and change; proper planning and project management.

why.a: Correct. The first principle.
why.b: Wrong. The text says the opposite: do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope.
why.c: Correct. Design systems for growth and change is a principle.
why.d: Wrong. Users are to be involved throughout, not held off.

prompt: True or false: the course text gives NINE principles of successful systems development, and 'justify systems as capital investments' is one of them.
explanation: Nine principles, and justifying systems as capital investments, with cost-benefit analysis, is the fifth.

why.true: Correct. Nine principles, and that is one.
why.false: Wrong. There are nine and this is one of them.

prompt: Match each principle with the reason the course text gives for it.

pairs.right: Accurate requirements, less resistance to change, more acceptance
Solve real business problems rather than merely apply technology
Structure and control, so the project is easier to manage and monitor

pairs.left: Establish standards for development and documentation
pairs.right: Consistency, quality and clarity, so systems are easier to maintain
Cost-benefit analysis shows whether benefits justify costs and risks

explanation: Five of the nine principles with their reasons. Users for acceptance, problem-solving for real problems, phases for control, standards for consistency, capital investment for cost-benefit justification.

prompt: Match each principle with what the course text says it achieves.

pairs.left: Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope
pairs.right: Prevents further waste when a project becomes too costly or risky
Smaller subsystems simplify development and reduce complexity

pairs.left: Design systems for growth and change
pairs.right: Flexible, scalable systems with a longer useful life
On schedule, within budget and meeting quality expectations

explanation: The remaining four principles. Cancel or revise to stop waste, divide to simplify, design for change to last, plan to stay on time and budget.

prompt: According to the course text, what does involving users throughout the process achieve?

options.text: It removes the need for testing
It ensures requirements are accurate, reduces resistance to change, and increases acceptance of the final system
It shortens the support phase to zero
It lets the analyst skip feasibility studies

explanation: Three payoffs: accurate requirements, less resistance, more acceptance.

why.a: Wrong. Testing remains one of the most critical steps whatever users do.
why.b: Correct. Those are the three benefits the text gives.
why.c: Wrong. Support continues for years after installation.
why.d: Wrong. Feasibility is still assessed in planning.

prompt: True or false: under the problem-solving principle, the course text says developers should apply the newest technology first and then look for a problem it solves.
explanation: The reverse: focus on real business problems rather than merely applying technology. Understand the problem, evaluate alternatives, pick the one with greatest benefit and least risk.

why.true: Wrong. The principle is to solve real business problems, not to apply technology for its own sake.
why.false: Correct. Understand the problem first, then choose the best option.

prompt: Which principle makes a project easier to manage, monitor and evaluate by dividing development into clearly defined phases?

options.text: Design systems for growth and change

explanation: Phases give structure and control, and each step is completed before the next. Divide and conquer, by contrast, splits the SYSTEM into subsystems, not the project into phases.

why.a: Correct. Establishing phases and activities provides structure and control.
why.b: Wrong. Divide and conquer breaks the system into components, not the project into phases.
why.c: Wrong. User involvement is about accuracy and acceptance.
why.d: Wrong. Designing for change is about flexibility and scalability.

prompt: True or false: the course text says standard methods, tools and documentation formats make systems easier to understand, maintain and enhance over time.
explanation: That is the point of establishing standards for development and documentation: consistency, quality and clarity.

why.true: Correct. That is the reason given for the standards principle.
why.false: Wrong. The text gives exactly this reason.

prompt: The principle 'justify systems as capital investments' relies on which analysis?
explanation: Information systems cost a great deal, so they are evaluated like other capital investments: do the expected benefits justify the costs and risks?

why.a: Wrong. Decision tables document business rules.
why.b: Correct. Cost-benefit analysis.
why.c: Wrong. Functional decomposition divides a system into subsystems.
why.d: Wrong. Balancing keeps DFD levels consistent.

prompt: A project has become too costly and no longer fits the organisation's goals. Which principle tells the team what to do?

options.text: Design systems for growth and change
Establish standards for development and documentation
Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope

explanation: Revising scope or cancelling prevents further waste of resources when a project becomes too costly, too risky or misaligned.

why.a: Wrong. That principle is about flexibility for the future.
why.b: Wrong. Standards are about consistency and quality.
why.c: Correct. Cancel or revise scope to stop the waste.
why.d: Wrong. Problem-solving is about focusing on real problems.

prompt: Proper planning and project management, in the course text, includes which two of these?
explanation: It includes realistic timelines, resource allocation, risk management and progress monitoring, and it keeps the project on schedule, within budget and to quality.

why.a: Correct. Risk management is included.
why.b: Wrong. No principle skips analysis.
why.c: Correct. Realistic timelines are included.
why.d: Wrong. User involvement is itself a principle.

prompt: A system is well understood and well defined, so the whole project can be planned in advance and run through a fixed sequence of phases. Which approach does the course text say suits it?
explanation: PREDICTIVE assumes the project can be planned in advance and followed through fixed phases; it suits well-understood systems. ADAPTIVE assumes it cannot, and works in short iterations.

why.a: Wrong. Adaptive is for projects that cannot be fully planned in advance.
why.b: Correct. Planned in advance, fixed sequence, well understood: predictive.
why.c: Wrong. Evolutionary prototyping is for requirements that evolve.
why.d: Wrong. Brainstorming is an idea-generating technique.

prompt: True or false: an adaptive approach handles changing requirements by developing in short cycles with continuous user feedback and incremental delivery.
explanation: Adaptive assumes the project cannot be planned in full in advance, so it is modified as it progresses, in short iterations.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's description of adaptive.
why.false: Wrong. Short cycles, continuous feedback and incremental delivery are exactly how adaptive works.

prompt: Match each predictive activity group with what it covers in the course text.

pairs.right: Planning, organising and scheduling the project
Understanding the business problem and defining requirements
Developing program structure and algorithms
Programming, testing and installing

explanation: Four activity groups in predictive development, and the text calls them PHASES. The fifth, support, belongs to the SDLC but not normally to the initial development project.

prompt: Which phase does the course text say is part of the overall SDLC but NOT normally considered part of the initial development project?
explanation: Support, the upgrading and maintenance after deployment, is in the SDLC but outside the initial development project, which runs from planning to implementation.

why.a: Wrong. Planning starts the development project.
why.b: Wrong. Analysis is inside the development project.
why.c: Wrong. Implementation ends the development project.
why.d: Correct. Support comes after deployment and is not normally part of the initial project.

prompt: True or false: the course text calls planning, analysis, design and implementation PHASES, which provide the framework for managing a project.
explanation: They are the phases, the management framework. Support is also in the SDLC but not normally part of the initial project.

why.true: Correct. They are called phases and provide the framework.
why.false: Wrong. The text uses exactly that word and purpose.

prompt: In the adaptive approach, what does the course text call the short repeated cycles, each producing a working version or component?
explanation: Iterations, also called sprints. Each produces a working version of the system or a component.

why.a: Wrong. Phases are the predictive framework.
why.b: Correct. Iterations or sprints.
why.c: Wrong. Adaptive emphasises working systems over documentation.
why.d: Wrong. Levels are DFD decomposition levels.

prompt: Which two of these are among the phases of the adaptive approach in the course text?

options.text: A single final testing phase at the very end
Formal sign-off before any code is written

explanation: The adaptive phases: initiation and requirements planning, iterative analysis and design, iterative development or construction, and continuous testing and quality assurance. Testing is continuous, not saved for the end.

why.a: Correct. Iterative analysis and design is one of the phases.
why.b: Wrong. Adaptive testing is CONTINUOUS; one late test phase is the Waterfall weakness.
why.c: Correct. Continuous testing and quality assurance is one of the phases.
why.d: Wrong. Formal sign-off at each phase is Waterfall's control, not adaptive.

prompt: True or false: in adaptive initiation and requirements planning, requirements are captured at a high level and prioritised by business value and urgency, often as user stories or feature lists.
explanation: The first adaptive phase sets the high-level scope, problem, objectives, stakeholders and major features, with requirements captured at a high level and prioritised.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's description of the first adaptive phase.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: Which model does the course text give as an example of the ADAPTIVE approach?
explanation: The Spiral model is the text's example of an adaptive approach. Waterfall and its two variants, Parallel and V-Shape, are predictive.

why.a: Wrong. Waterfall is the classic predictive model.
why.b: Wrong. The V-Shape model is a Waterfall variant, so predictive.
why.c: Correct. The Spiral model.
why.d: Wrong. The Parallel model is a Waterfall variant, so predictive.

prompt: Complete the course text's comparison table: match each row heading with its entry.

pairs.right: Defined upfront
Evolve over time
Detailed documentation
Strong user involvement and collaboration
Linear and structured

explanation: The table's rows: upfront against evolving requirements; linear against iterative; documentation against user involvement; limited flexibility against working systems over documentation.

prompt: In the course text's table, which characteristic belongs to the PREDICTIVE approach?

options.text: Emphasis on working systems over extensive documentation

explanation: Predictive: requirements upfront, linear and structured, detailed documentation, limited flexibility. The other three options are all adaptive.

why.a: Wrong. Iterative and incremental is adaptive.
why.b: Wrong. Working systems over documentation is adaptive.
why.c: Correct. Limited flexibility is the predictive row.
why.d: Wrong. Evolving requirements are adaptive.

prompt: True or false: the course text warns that selecting the wrong development approach can lead to cost overruns, delays, user dissatisfaction and system failure.
explanation: The approach decides how requirements are gathered, changes managed, risks controlled and the system delivered, so choosing wrongly is costly.

why.true: Correct. Those four consequences are named.
why.false: Wrong. The text lists exactly these consequences.

prompt: The course text organises the SDLC into five major phases. Which list is correct, in order?
explanation: Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Support. Planning comes before analysis, and support closes the cycle.

why.a: Correct. The five phases in order.
why.b: Wrong. Planning comes first, and testing is inside implementation, not its own phase.
why.c: Wrong. Analysis comes before design.
why.d: Wrong. That resembles the adaptive phases, not the five SDLC phases.

prompt: Which two of these are primary objectives of project planning in the course text?

options.text: Identify the scope of the new system

explanation: Three objectives: identify scope, ensure feasibility, and develop a schedule, resource plan and budget for the rest of the project.

why.a: Correct. Identifying scope is an objective of planning.
why.b: Wrong. Constructing software is implementation.
why.c: Correct. Ensuring feasibility is an objective of planning.
why.d: Wrong. Training users is implementation.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five activities of project planning in the course text?
explanation: The five planning activities: define the problem, produce the schedule, confirm feasibility, staff the project, launch the project. Converting data is implementation.

why.a: Wrong choice, because defining the problem IS a planning activity.
why.b: Wrong choice, because confirming feasibility IS a planning activity.
why.c: Correct. Converting data is one of the five IMPLEMENTATION activities.
why.d: Wrong choice, because staffing the project IS a planning activity.

prompt: True or false: 'launch the project' is one of the five activities of project planning.
explanation: Planning ends by launching the project, after defining the problem, scheduling, confirming feasibility and staffing.

why.true: Correct. Launching the project is the last planning activity.
why.false: Wrong. It is one of the five.

prompt: On page 21 the course text says feasibility analysis in project planning investigates five kinds of feasibility. Which of these is NOT among them?
explanation: The page 21 list: economic, organisational, technical, resource and schedule. (Page 24 gives a slightly different list for feasibility studies: technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule.) Marketing appears in neither.

why.a: Wrong choice, because organisational feasibility IS in the page 21 list.
why.b: Wrong choice, because resource feasibility IS in the page 21 list.
why.c: Correct. Marketing feasibility is in neither of the text's lists.
why.d: Wrong choice, because schedule feasibility IS in the list.

prompt: According to the course text, which two KEY WORDS drive the analysis phase?
explanation: Analysis is essentially a discovery process: understand and document the business needs and processing requirements.

why.a: Wrong. Not the text's key words.
why.b: Correct. Discovery and understanding.
why.c: Wrong. Construction and testing are implementation.
why.d: Wrong. Maintenance and enhancement are support.

prompt: Which two of these are among the six primary activities of the analysis phase?

options.text: Build a prototype for discovery of requirements

explanation: The six: gather information, define requirements, prioritise requirements, build a discovery prototype, generate and evaluate alternatives, review recommendations with management.

why.a: Correct. Prioritising requirements is an analysis activity.
why.b: Wrong. Network design is one of the DESIGN activities.
why.c: Correct. A discovery prototype is an analysis activity.
why.d: Wrong. Installation is implementation.

prompt: True or false: 'review recommendations with management' is one of the six analysis phase activities.
explanation: It is the last of the six: after generating and evaluating alternatives, the analyst reviews the recommendations with management.

why.true: Correct. It closes the analysis activities.
why.false: Wrong. It is one of the six.

prompt: How is information gathered in the analysis phase? Choose the two methods the course text names.

options.text: Observing users as they do their work

explanation: Four sources: observing users, interviewing them, reading existing documents, and reviewing existing automated systems.

why.a: Correct. Observation is one of the four.
why.b: Wrong. The text never allows guessing; the analyst must not assume.
why.c: Correct. Reviewing existing systems is one of the four.
why.d: Wrong. Not a method in the text.

prompt: Match each SDLC phase with its objective in the course text.

pairs.right: Identify scope, ensure feasibility, and produce the schedule, resource plan and budget
Understand and document the business needs and processing requirements
Design the solution system from the requirements and decisions of analysis
A reliable, fully functional system, with all users trained
Keep the system running productively in the years after installation

explanation: One objective per phase. Notice implementation includes training users, and support is measured in years.

prompt: Developing the detailed algorithms and data structures required for software development is which kind of design?
explanation: HIGH-LEVEL design is the architecture: software components, databases, interface, operating environment. LOW-LEVEL design is the detail: algorithms and data structures.

why.a: Wrong. High-level design is the architectural structure.
why.b: Correct. Detailed algorithms and data structures are low-level design.
why.c: Wrong. Logical design is a design phase deliverable, not the text's name for this.
why.d: Wrong. Discovery prototyping is a fact-finding technique.

prompt: True or false: high-level design develops an architectural structure for the software components, databases, user interface and operating environment.
explanation: High-level is the architecture; low-level is the detailed algorithms and data structures.

why.false: Wrong. That is exactly the text's definition of high-level design.

prompt: Which two of these are among the five major DESIGN activities?

options.text: Design and integrate the system controls

explanation: The five design activities: application architecture, network, user and system interfaces, database, and system controls.

why.a: Correct. Database design is one of the five.
why.b: Wrong. Gathering information is an ANALYSIS activity.
why.c: Correct. System controls are one of the five.
why.d: Wrong. Verifying and testing is an IMPLEMENTATION activity.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five major IMPLEMENTATION activities?

options.text: Train users and document the system

explanation: The five: construct software components, verify and test, convert data, train users and document the system, install the system. Prioritising requirements belongs to analysis.

why.a: Wrong choice, because constructing components IS implementation.
why.b: Wrong choice, because converting data IS implementation.
why.c: Correct. Prioritising requirements is an analysis activity.
why.d: Wrong choice, because training and documenting IS implementation.

prompt: True or false: the course text defines installation as the process of turning off the old system and turning on the new one.
explanation: Installation is the last of the five implementation activities, and the conversion approach decides how the switch is made.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's definition.
why.false: Wrong. The text defines installation exactly so.

prompt: True or false: the course text says most organisations spend more time and attention on testing than on writing the programs in the first place.
explanation: Because the cost of bugs can be immense, testing is one of the most critical steps in implementation.

why.true: Correct. The text says exactly this.
why.false: Wrong. The text says testing gets MORE time than writing the programs.

prompt: Match each conversion approach with its description.

pairs.right: The new system immediately replaces the old
Both systems run for a month or two until the new one has no bugs
Small parts of the new system gradually replace small parts of the old
A small group of users uses the new system before wider use

explanation: Direct is immediate; parallel runs both; phased swaps piece by piece; pilot tries it on a small group first.

prompt: A bank runs its old and new systems side by side for two months until it is clear the new one has no bugs. Which conversion approach is this?
explanation: Both systems running together for a month or two is parallel conversion: the safest, and the most costly.

why.a: Wrong. Direct cutover replaces the old system immediately, with no overlap.
why.b: Wrong. Pilot gives the new system to a small group first.
why.c: Wrong. Phased replaces small parts gradually, not the whole system in parallel.
why.d: Correct. Both run together: parallel.

prompt: What does the course text call one of the most important aspects of conversion?

options.text: Developing a training plan to teach users the new system and manage the changes it brings
Deleting all the old data first
Writing a new requirements definition document

explanation: Users must be taught the new system, and the training plan also helps manage the changes it introduces.

why.a: Correct. The training plan.
why.b: Wrong. Data is converted, not deleted first.
why.c: Wrong. Requirements are documented in analysis, not at conversion.
why.d: Wrong. Brainstorming generates ideas in JRP.

prompt: Which two of these are among the three major support activities?

options.text: Support the users through a help desk

explanation: Three support activities: maintain the system, enhance the system, support the users through a help desk.

why.a: Correct. Enhancing is one of the three.
why.b: Wrong. Staffing is a planning activity.
why.c: Correct. The help desk is one of the three.
why.d: Wrong. Alternatives are generated in analysis.

prompt: Match each piece of work with where the course text puts it.

pairs.left: Fixing a bug in the payroll calculation
pairs.right: Maintaining the system

pairs.left: A major change forced by new government regulations
pairs.right: Enhancing the system

pairs.left: Helping a user who cannot log in
pairs.right: Supporting the users through the help desk

pairs.left: Turning off the old system and turning on the new one
pairs.right: Installation, an implementation activity

explanation: Maintaining covers fixing bugs and minor adjustments; enhancing covers MAJOR changes from regulations, the business environment, markets, competition or infrastructure; the help desk supports users. Switching systems over is installation, which happens in implementation, before support begins.

prompt: True or false: the course text says training new users and maintaining current documentation are important elements of the help desk activity.
explanation: A help desk is support staff available for any technical or processing problem, and training and documentation are named as important elements of it.

why.false: Wrong. The text names both as elements of the help desk activity.

prompt: Match each deliverable with the SDLC phase that produces it, from the course text's table of deliverables.

pairs.right: Planning
Analysis

pairs.left: Logical design, technical design and test plans
pairs.right: Design

pairs.left: End-user training materials and contingency plans
pairs.right: Implementation
Support

explanation: Planning proposes, analysis specifies requirements, design produces the designs and test plans, implementation delivers the system with its training materials and plans, support reports on maintenance.

prompt: Which set of deliverables does the course text give for the ANALYSIS phase?

options.text: Detailed system requirements, revised cost and benefits analysis, revised schedule
Maintenance reports and updated system documentation
System elements, contingency plans and a maintenance plan
Logical design, technical design and test plans

explanation: Analysis delivers the detailed requirements and revises the cost-benefit analysis and schedule.

why.a: Correct. The analysis deliverables.
why.b: Wrong. These are support phase deliverables.
why.c: Wrong. These are implementation deliverables.
why.d: Wrong. These are design deliverables.

prompt: True or false: test plans are a deliverable of the DESIGN phase in the course text's table.
explanation: Design delivers the logical design, technical design, test plans, and a revised cost-benefit analysis and schedule. Tests are PLANNED in design and CARRIED OUT in implementation.

why.true: Correct. Test plans are listed under design.
why.false: Wrong. The table puts test plans under design, even though testing itself happens in implementation.

prompt: Which two of these are PLANNING phase deliverables in the course text's table?
explanation: Planning deliverables: project proposal and recommendation, investigation report, analysis of alternatives, cost and benefit analysis, schedule, recommendation.

why.a: Correct. Analysis of alternatives is a planning deliverable.
why.b: Wrong. Cutover or phase-in is an implementation deliverable.
why.c: Correct. Cost and benefit analysis is a planning deliverable.
why.d: Wrong. Updated documentation is a support deliverable.

prompt: 'Cutover or phase-in' appears in the course text's table as a deliverable of which phase?
explanation: Implementation delivers system elements, implementation plans, contingency plans, training materials, a maintenance plan, operations plans, and cutover or phase-in.

why.a: Wrong. Planning delivers proposals and analyses, not the switch-over.
why.b: Wrong. Design delivers designs and test plans.
why.c: Correct. Cutover or phase-in is how implementation ends.
why.d: Wrong. Support delivers maintenance reports and documentation.

prompt: True or false: the support phase deliverables are maintenance reports and updated system documentation.
explanation: Two deliverables for support: maintenance reports and updated system documentation.

why.false: Wrong. The table gives exactly these two.

prompt: Match each kind of feasibility with what it evaluates, as the course text describes feasibility studies in the planning phase.

pairs.right: Availability of technology and skills
Cost-benefit analysis
User acceptance and organisational impact
Compliance with laws and regulations
Ability to finish within the required timeframe

explanation: Five kinds, each with its question: can we build it, is it worth it, will it be used, is it lawful, can we finish in time.

prompt: Feasibility studies belong particularly to which SDLC phase?
explanation: Feasibility is confirmed before the project is committed to, so it belongs to planning.

why.a: Correct. The text places feasibility studies in planning.
why.b: Wrong. By design the project is already judged feasible.
why.c: Wrong. Far too late to decide whether to proceed.
why.d: Wrong. Support follows installation.

prompt: True or false: feasibility studies let management decide whether to proceed, modify or abandon a project by identifying constraints early.
explanation: They reduce risk and prevent wasted resources, so only projects with a reasonable chance of success move forward.

why.false: Wrong. That is exactly what the text says feasibility studies are for.

prompt: True or false: in the course text, testing is a separate SDLC phase between design and implementation.
explanation: The five phases are planning, analysis, design, implementation and support. Testing is one of the implementation activities ('verify and test'), and in predictive development implementation means programming, testing and installing.

why.true: Wrong. Testing is inside implementation, not its own phase.
why.false: Correct. Testing is an implementation activity.

prompt: True or false: the predictive approach suits systems whose requirements are unclear and changing.
explanation: Predictive suits systems that are well understood and well defined. Unclear, changing requirements call for the adaptive approach.

why.true: Wrong. That describes when to use ADAPTIVE.
why.false: Correct. Predictive is for well-understood, well-defined systems.

prompt: Which two statements about the adaptive approach are true, according to the course text?

options.text: Its short cycles are called iterations or sprints
It completes each phase fully before the next begins
The Spiral model is an example of it
The V-Shape model is an example of it

explanation: Adaptive works in iterations, or sprints, each producing working software; Spiral is the text's example. Completing each phase first, and the V-Shape model, are predictive.

why.a: Correct. Iterations or sprints.
why.b: Wrong. That is the predictive way.
why.c: Correct. The Spiral model is the text's adaptive example.
why.d: Wrong. The V-Shape model is a Waterfall variant, so predictive.

prompt: Which phase's primary objective is to understand and document the business needs and processing requirements of the new system?
explanation: Analysis: understand and document the business needs. Planning identifies scope and feasibility; design designs the solution.

why.a: Wrong. Planning identifies scope, ensures feasibility and sets the schedule and budget.
why.b: Correct. That is the objective of analysis.
why.c: Wrong. Design builds the solution from the requirements analysis produced.
why.d: Wrong. Support keeps the system running after installation.
